rationale: A wins because it mostly turns the supplied facts into reporter-shaped tensions instead of decorating them with brand mythology. Its best angle, "Liquid Death bets a flagship store can do what 120,000 grocery aisles can't," finds the actual contradiction in the update. B has useful bones, but lines like "a brand that grew through cans-on-shelves and viral video" and "brand built on shock marketing" import outside assumptions; that is how a pitch gets cute and then gets fact-checked into paste.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now" overclaims exclusivity; the update says limited-edition canned water, not store-exclusive canned water.
"the limited-edition can launches alongside the store opening" is stronger than the facts supplied; the store sells it, but no launch timing is given.
"near-total retail penetration" is sloppy inflation. The update gives ~120,000 retail doors, not market saturation.
The fourth angle is the weakest: "limited-run SKU strategy" may be real, but it needs proof before it earns its own pitch lane.
gaps_in_B: "converts to a B Corp" is imprecise. The fact is Certified B Corp this quarter; certification is not a corporate conversion.
"DTC-native and 'anti-marketing' brands" is not in the update. It may sound plausible because the brand is Liquid Death, but plausible is not permission.
"grew through cans-on-shelves and viral video" imports outside history. The supplied fact is 120,000 retail doors, not viral growth mechanics.
"brand built on shock marketing" and "death-themed marketing" make the B Corp angle depend on unsupplied brand-color commentary instead of the actual certification and donation facts.
